transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-01-05
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Arjun Patel (Redwood SE); Samir Rao (Redwood SE); Lara Gomez (Oakridge, Head of ML); Tom Wu (Oakridge, Infra Lead); Priya Menon (Oakridge, Security); Ethan Ross (Oakridge, Product)

Summary (auto): quick review of last week's pilot telemetry, discuss autoscaling policy for Dedicated, plan burst capacity playbook, agree next tests.

Topics: Dedicated sizing, autoscale cooldowns, burst capacity, p95/p99 tail, KV cache warmup, quantization tradeoffs, security checklist.

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll do a quick sync on the POC telemetry and then dig into sizing and burst behaviour. arjun's got the latest load tests to show.
[00:18] Arjun Patel: cool, morning/afternoon; quick disclaimer the numbers are from the test cluster which mirrors your nightly job traffic, but slight diffs in sequence length distribution. we simulated both steady state and a 10x burst for two 15-minute windows.
[00:34] Lara Gomez: great, we need to understand how committed capacity behaves during those bursts, and how fallback to hosted variants would work if we blow the pool.
[00:43] Tom Wu: yes, also want to see p99 spikes - last week we saw a few 2s spikes which hurt our SLA.
[00:50] Arjun Patel: right; so steady state we saw p95 around 180-220ms for the 2k-token baseline prompt with a quantized LLM on A100-ish sim, p99 averaged 520ms but there were a few tails up to 1.1s during cold KV cache periods. during 10x burst the average per-token throughput dropped and queueing increased; with our default autoscale policy (scale step = +4 GPUs, cooldown 300s) we recovered to near steady throughput in ~6 minutes.
[01:20] Ethan Ross: six minutes is a long time for customer-facing flows; can we make it faster?
[01:24] Samir Rao: you can tune the policy — smaller scale steps with shorter cooldowns reduce tail but increase cost oscillation. we recommended a hybrid policy: fast initial buffer (burst capacity) for short spikes then gradual scaling for sustained load. basically a two-tier policy: reserve small burst pool and autoscale above that.
[01:44] Priya Menon: from security side, if we reserve burst nodes, do logs and keys stay in your private control plane? we need to be sure no ephemeral host leaks logs.
[01:52] Maya Chen: yes, for Dedicated the KMS is customer-managed if you want and audit logs are streamed to your SIEM; the burst nodes are within the same VPC/capability and follow same encryption and log routing. we'll add a diagram to the playbook.
[02:05] Lara Gomez: what about caching? we saw higher latency when the KV cache wasn't warmed. how does Redwood handle prefix caching across scaled nodes?
[02:13] Arjun Patel: good q; we shard KV cache across nodes but we also have cross-node prefetch and a warmup strategy: when new nodes come up they can fetch the most recent hot keys from the prefix cache service. warmup depends on model context size and typical prefixes; in our stress run warmup added ~350ms for the first few requests on a new node which contributed to that 1.1s tail. could be improved by pre-warming during burst if we predict the traffic.
[02:42] Tom Wu: can we control pre-warm policy? like pre-warm only for the top 5 prefixes?
[02:46] Arjun Patel: yep we can configure that. typical recommendation is top-N prefixes per route, TTL, and an aggressive prefetch during expected bursts. we'll include examples in the playbook.
[02:56] Lara Gomez: curious on the math for sizing: we asked for 12 concurrent workers originally, you recommended 16 with a burst pool of 4. what's the buffer calc?
[03:06] Samir Rao: the sizing started from your steady tps (tokens/sec) and p95 latency target; we assume average seq len, batching efficiency at your qps, and kernel throughput. buffer = safety factor (1.25) + headroom for burst concurrency. so 16 handles 95% of traffic with typical batching; burst pool of 4 gives headroom for 2x to 4x short spikes without immediate autoscale.
[03:25] Tom Wu: do we pay for burst pool even if unused?
[03:28] Maya Chen: pricing options: committed reserved capacity covers baseline; burst nodes can be configured as on-demand with minute-level billing in Dedicated or as pre-committed low-cost nodes for heavy customers. for the pilot we can model both in the spreadsheet. I'll attach both cost curves.
[03:44] Ethan Ross: what about cooldown and scale-in behaviour? we don't want thrash if load oscillates.
[03:48] Arjun Patel: scale-in uses asymmetric cooldowns; scale-out is faster, scale-in uses longer cooldowns and checks for sustained low utilization across N intervals. that prevents flapping. we can tune threshold (utilization pct), evaluation window, and max scale step.
[04:05] Lara Gomez: any impact of quantization choices? we tested 4-bit and saw slightly higher variance in p99 tails.
[04:12] Samir Rao: quantization reduces memory/cost but can impact kernel selection and per-token latency; sometimes increases p99 due to VLLM fallback patterns or reorders. for production we recommend 4-bit for non-latency critical routes, and 8-bit for low-latency routes. also sequence length distribution matters more with quantized kernels.
[04:30] Tom Wu: on the subject of fallbacks — if dedicated runs out of capacity what happens?
[04:35] Maya Chen: by policy we can fail open to a hosted variant (lower latency SLA) or queue requests, or return an explicit error. common pattern is to route non-sensitive traffic to hosted or to degrade model (e.g., smaller model) as automatic fallback. your choice.
[04:50] Priya Menon: open-hosted fallback raises data residency questions; we need to ensure PHI doesn't leave our VPC.
[04:55] Maya Chen: agreed — we can restrict fallback to only non-sensitive routes; for sensitive routes we keep strict capacity or return 429. We'll mark routes in the playbook with sensitivity labels.
[05:06] Lara Gomez: back to tests — what does the 8-hour stress test look like?
[05:10] Arjun Patel: we plan 3 phases: ramp, sustained high plateau with periodic micro-bursts, and a 10x mega-burst window. we'll capture per-node metrics, queue lengths, cache hit-rates, and tail latencies. we'll also record kernel-level metrics and NVTX-charts.
[05:22] Ethan Ross: good; please include the trace samples so we can compare our ingest pipeline traces.
[05:25] Samir Rao: noted.
[05:27] Maya Chen: next steps recap: we'll send updated sizing + playbook + cost models; Arjun will run stress tests and share results; Tom will share Oakridge telemetry. Any blockers?
[05:36] Tom Wu: only thing is procurement — assuming pilot looks ok we need committed pricing for burst nodes; procurement wants a 30-day window.
[05:42] Maya Chen: we'll include a pilot pricing appendix that outlines burst options and month-to-month terms.
[05:46] Lara Gomez: also security will want SOC2 artifacts and key management docs — Priya will send a list.
[05:50] Priya Menon: yes, I'll send a list of required attestations and any encryption policies.
[05:55] Maya Chen: perfect, thanks everyone. we'll follow up by Thursday with artifacts.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional word swaps and partial names (e.g., NVTX pronounced "N-V-T-X" transcribed as N V T X), timestamps approximate.

References/links mentioned: Redwood sizing spreadsheet (link shared in chat), playbook draft (to be attached), sample traces (will be uploaded to S3 link).

End of transcript.
